q: בת 84, ברקע יתר לחץ דם, עודף משקל, היפרתירואידיזם, מעשנת כבדה. במעקב שגרתי במרפאה נצפו דפורמציות באצבעות כפות הידיים. מה מגורמי הרקע שלה הוא גורם סיכון לממצאים שנראו בידיים?
o: עודף משקל
יתר לחץ דם
היפרתירואידיזם
עישון
explanation:
**Obesity is associated with hand osteoarthritis**, even though the hand is not weight-bearing. The image allows the deformities in the question to be considered, but does not itself establish the risk factor; Hazzard explicitly states the obesity association (p. 780).
“Obesity is also associated with having an increased risk of developing hand and foot OA.” (p. 780).

**A. Overweight.** Correct, the source explicitly links this factor to hand OA. It supports the official choice without inferring the mechanism from the image (p. 780).
**B. Hypertension.** Wrong, according to the official key. In the Rotterdam study, the association with hand OA was weak and disappeared after BMI adjustment; this specific finding must not be converted into a general claim of no association (Dahaghin et al., Results).
**C. Hyperthyroidism.** Wrong, according to the official key. Hazzard establishes the obesity association here but does not directly compare it with hyperthyroidism for the depicted deformities; the study must not be presented as disproving this option (p. 780).
**D. Smoking.** Wrong, according to the official key. The positive obesity association does not prove absence of a smoking association. Neither an etiological diagnosis nor a causal smoking relationship can be inferred from the hand image (p. 780).

Missing step: A direct, deciding comparison between obesity, hypertension, hyperthyroidism, and smoking for this hand phenotype is lacking. The inherited review checked Hazzard 8e, a whole-book search, and the Rotterdam study; a further open search did not supply that comparison. Its Downloads search found no deciding source, and its Clalit route required a new login.

Source: Hazzard 8e, p. 780; Dahaghin S et al. Do metabolic factors add to the effect of overweight on hand osteoarthritis? Ann Rheum Dis. 2007;66:916–920, Results. doi:10.1136/ard.2005.045724; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1955104/.

q: גבר בן 78 שנים עם היסטוריה של סוכרת הופקד לאשפוז עם דלקת ריאות. בחקירה קלינית: דופק 105/דקה, לחץ דם 92/58, טמפרטורה 38.5°C. למרות טיפול אנטיביוטי מתאים, המטופל אינו מגיב כצפוי ותמותתו עולה משמעותית. איזה מהגורמים הביולוגיים הבאים מסביר בעיקר את תגובת החיסון המוגבלת בקשישים?
o: ירידה בתפקוד תאי T ובוגרות תאי B
עלייה בסינתזת אנטיגנים
הגברת הפקת ציטוקינים פרו-דלקתיים
ירידה בשיעור ההתחלקות של תאים דם לבנים
explanation: בשיוך (senescence), תאי T מראים ירידה בתפקוד התגובה החיסונית ותאי B מראים ירידה בוגרות. זה מסביר תגובה חלשה לזיהום ולחיסונים בקשישים. הופעת הזיהום הקשה וחוסר התגובה לטיפול משקפת חיסון חלוש. (Hazzard's - Immunosenescence)
ref: Hazzard Ch 1 — BIOLOGY OF AGING AND LONGEVITY

q: A 79-year-old woman with sarcopenia is receiving nutritional advice and asks what to add to improve muscle strength and function. Which intervention is the evidence-supported cornerstone described by Hazzard?
o: A regular aerobic walking program as the main exercise component
A regular resistance exercise program started with expert professional supervision
Vitamin D supplementation for muscle function without severe vitamin deficiency
Growth hormone treatment to increase the amount of skeletal muscle
explanation:
**Resistance exercise** has compelling evidence for improving muscle function and mass in sarcopenia (p. 737). Repetitive movements using weights or elastic bands target muscle strength and power: "Including resistance exercise is key to improve muscle function." (p. 737)

**A. A regular aerobic walking program as the main exercise component.** Wrong, the source distinguishes usual cardiovascular activities such as walking from the resistance component required to improve muscle function in sarcopenia (p. 737).
**B. A regular resistance exercise program started with expert professional supervision.** Correct, resistance exercise targets the function being treated; the source advises starting under expert exercise or physical-therapy supervision to teach correct performance and avoid injury (p. 737).
**C. Vitamin D supplementation for muscle function without severe vitamin deficiency.** Wrong, vitamin D has not been shown to improve muscle function in sarcopenic patients, with possible benefit described in severe deficiency rather than the situation proposed (p. 737).
**D. Growth hormone treatment to increase the amount of skeletal muscle.** Wrong, growth hormone is among the hormonal treatments whose trials showed negative results; it is not the source’s evidence-supported treatment cornerstone (p. 737).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 737.
ref: Hazzard Ch 49 — MUSCLE AGING AND SARCOPENIA

q: חולה עם דמנציה הוגדרה בישראל כחולה הנוטה למות שאינה בעלת כשרות. לפני הכרעה לגבי רצונה בהארכת חיים, איזה מידע יש לברר לפי סעיף 5(ב)?
o: את רצון הבת שהביעה העדפה לטיפול המרחיב ביותר
את רצון הבן שהביע העדפה לטיפול המצמצם ביותר
הנחיות תקפות, החלטת מיופה כוח או החלטת ועדה
את העדפת הצוות במשמרת שהכיר אותה לאחרונה
explanation:
בירור **רצון חולה שאינה בעלת כשרות** נעשה במסלולים שהחוק מונה. הנחיות מקדימות תקפות, החלטת מיופה כוח לפי תנאי החוק או החלטת ועדה הם מסלולי הבירור בסעיף, ולא העדפת קרוב או איש צוות כשלעצמה (עמ׳ 5, סעיף 5(ב)).
"הנחיות רפואיות מקדימות שנתן שמתקיימות בהן הוראות סעיפים 33 ו-34(א);" (עמ׳ 5).
"החלטה של מיופה כוחו שניתנה לפי ייפוי כוח שמתקיימות בו הוראות סעיפים 38 ו-39(א);" (עמ׳ 5).

**א. את רצון הבת שהביעה העדפה לטיפול המרחיב ביותר.** שגויה, העדפת הבת כשלעצמה אינה אחד המסלולים; יש לברר סמכות ומידע בדבר רצון החולה (עמ׳ 5).
**ב. את רצון הבן שהביע העדפה לטיפול המצמצם ביותר.** שגויה, העדפת הבן כשלעצמה אינה מספיקה גם כשהוא מבקש טיפול מצומצם (עמ׳ 5).
**ג. הנחיות תקפות, החלטת מיופה כוח או החלטת ועדה.** נכונה, אלה המסלולים המפורטים בחוק ויש לבדוק את תוקפם ואת תנאיהם (עמ׳ 5).
**ד. את העדפת הצוות במשמרת שהכיר אותה לאחרונה.** שגויה, העדפה של הצוות אינה מחליפה את בירור הרצון במנגנונים שבסעיף (עמ׳ 5).

מקור: חוק החולה הנוטה למות, תשס_ו-2005.pdf, עמ׳ 5.
ref: Hazzard Ch 7 — DECISION MAKING AND ADVANCE CARE PLANNING: WHAT MATTERS MOST

q: An 84-year-old woman with frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 6), COPD requiring home oxygen, and stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22) lives alone, uses a walker, and receives help from her daughter with shopping and medication. She takes furosemide 40 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, and albuterol as needed. Potassium is 5.8, creatinine 2.8 (stable), and bicarbonate 18. She feels well apart from mild fatigue. Which change addresses Hazzard's contraindication to continuing mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist treatment?
o: Stop spironolactone given hyperkalemia and renal dysfunction.
Continue spironolactone while adding oral sodium bicarbonate.
Continue spironolactone while reducing the dose of furosemide.
Continue spironolactone while adding a potassium-binding agent.
explanation:
**Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists** are contraindicated in significant renal dysfunction or preexisting hyperkalemia (p. 1181). The source states, "These agents are contraindicated in patients with significant renal dysfunction (creatinine ≥ 2.5 mg/dL) or preexisting hyperkalemia" (p. 1181). The question asks which change removes that contraindicated exposure, rather than ranking a complete hyperkalemia treatment plan.

**A. Stop spironolactone given hyperkalemia and renal dysfunction.** Correct, this removes the mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist exposure in the setting of the stated contraindications (p. 1181).
**B. Continue spironolactone while adding oral sodium bicarbonate.** Wrong, adding bicarbonate while continuing the drug does not implement the source's contraindication to that exposure (p. 1181).
**C. Continue spironolactone while reducing the dose of furosemide.** Wrong, reducing another diuretic leaves the contraindicated mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist exposure in place (p. 1181).
**D. Continue spironolactone while adding a potassium-binding agent.** Wrong, adding another potassium treatment leaves the contraindicated exposure in place; it is not the withdrawal asked for (p. 1181).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1181.
ref: Hazzard Ch 22 — MEDICATION PRESCRIBING AND DE-PRESCRIBING

q: An 88-year-old man with mild dementia, BPH, osteoarthritis, and insomnia has become increasingly confused over three days and no longer recognizes family. One week ago he started diphenhydramine 50 mg at bedtime and oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily. Vital signs are stable and CAM screening is positive. Which medication plan applies Beers 2023 guidance to minimize his anticholinergic burden?
o: Discontinue both diphenhydramine and oxybutynin, then reassess symptoms.
Replace diphenhydramine with oral doxylamine and continue oxybutynin.
Replace oxybutynin with oral tolterodine and continue diphenhydramine.
Continue both diphenhydramine and oxybutynin while monitoring symptoms.
explanation:
**Concurrent anticholinergic drugs** increase the risk of cognitive decline, delirium, and falls or fractures. Beers lists both diphenhydramine and oxybutynin as strongly anticholinergic and recommends minimizing the number of such drugs (pp. 2070, 2074). "Use of more than one medication with anticholinergic properties increases the risk of cognitive decline, delirium, and falls or fractures." (p. 2070).

**A. Discontinue both diphenhydramine and oxybutynin, then reassess symptoms.** Correct, this removes both listed exposures and implements the recommendation to minimize anticholinergic drugs (pp. 2070, 2074).
**B. Replace diphenhydramine with oral doxylamine and continue oxybutynin.** Wrong, doxylamine is also strongly anticholinergic, so the substitution leaves two listed drugs in use (p. 2074).
**C. Replace oxybutynin with oral tolterodine and continue diphenhydramine.** Wrong, tolterodine is also strongly anticholinergic, so this substitution retains two listed drugs in use (p. 2074).
**D. Continue both diphenhydramine and oxybutynin while monitoring symptoms.** Wrong, monitoring without reducing exposure does not implement the recommendation to minimize concurrent anticholinergic drugs (p. 2070).

Source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023, pp. 2070, 2074.
label: Source: AGS Beers 2023 · pp. 2066, 2070, 2074; Tables 3, 5, 7

q: A 75-year-old woman with recently diagnosed mild cognitive impairment developed worsening confusion after starting solifenacin for urgency urinary incontinence. Her clinician plans to replace the antimuscarinic with a beta-3 agonist. Which prescription matches that class in Hazzard?
o: Oxybutynin for urgency urinary incontinence
Mirabegron for urgency urinary incontinence
Tolterodine for urgency urinary incontinence
Solifenacin for urgency urinary incontinence
explanation:
**Bladder antimuscarinics** have anticholinergic effects, and Hazzard warns about drug-induced delirium in patients with dementia. Table 47-12 distinguishes **mirabegron**, a beta-3 agonist, from the antimuscarinic drugs (pp. 712–713). "Mirabegron (Myrbetriq)" (p. 712).

**A. Oxybutynin for urgency urinary incontinence.** Wrong, oxybutynin is listed under antimuscarinics and would not accomplish the specified change of class (p. 712).
**B. Mirabegron for urgency urinary incontinence.** Correct, mirabegron is listed as a beta-3 agonist, matching the planned replacement class (p. 712).
**C. Tolterodine for urgency urinary incontinence.** Wrong, tolterodine is an antimuscarinic, so it retains the class the clinician intends to replace (p. 712).
**D. Solifenacin for urgency urinary incontinence.** Wrong, solifenacin is an antimuscarinic and is the current drug, so this does not implement the proposed class change (p. 712).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 712, 713.

q: A 77-year-old woman reports dizziness when wearing high-necked sweaters or adjusting necklaces. Yesterday she briefly lost consciousness during hair washing at a salon. She has coronary artery disease treated with stenting and hypertension, and takes aspirin 81 mg daily, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. If contraindications are excluded, which test directly evaluates suspected carotid sinus hypersensitivity?
o: Carotid ultrasound with Doppler blood-flow assessment.
Carotid sinus massage with continuous monitoring.
Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring with ambulatory ECG recording.
Tilt-table testing with an infusion of isoproterenol.
explanation:
**Carotid sinus hypersensitivity** is evaluated by monitored carotid sinus massage. Mechanical neck pressure can provoke the syndrome, and the procedure requires screening for contraindications such as carotid occlusion, heart block, bruits, or a recent cerebrovascular event or myocardial infarction (p. 669). "It is diagnosed by carotid sinus massage sequentially on each side of the neck while blood pressure and heart rate are being monitored." (p. 669).

**A. Carotid ultrasound with Doppler blood-flow assessment.** Wrong, arterial imaging does not test the reflex response to carotid sinus stimulation, and the source discourages routine carotid imaging for syncope (p. 672).
**B. Carotid sinus massage with continuous monitoring.** Correct, this is the specific provocative test described for the suspected hypersensitive reflex (p. 669).
**C. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring with ambulatory ECG recording.** Wrong, ambulatory ECG seeks symptom-rhythm correlation and does not directly provoke the neck-pressure reflex; absence of symptoms during recording limits its exclusion value (pp. 671–672).
**D. Tilt-table testing with an infusion of isoproterenol.** Wrong, tilt testing evaluates responses to posture change and is reserved for selected unexplained cases; it does not directly test the localized trigger described (p. 672).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 669, 672, 671.
ref: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 669, Carotid sinus hypersensitivity; p. 672, Noncardiac syncope
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 669, Carotid sinus hypersensitivity; p. 672, Noncardiac syncope

q: A 78-year-old woman with moderate dementia (MMSE 18/30) has lost 8 kg in six months and now needs help bathing. She denies complaints. She takes donepezil 10 mg, metformin 500 mg twice daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg. Albumin is 2.8, hemoglobin 10.2, and TSH is normal. Her daughter asks about appetite stimulants. After reversible causes have been addressed, which approach is supported without assuming proven benefit from an appetite stimulant?
o: Use mirtazapine for weight gain without establishing depression.
Use megestrol for expected gains in function and quality of life.
Use dronabinol for established clinical benefits in older adults.
Adjust the meal environment and provide feeding assistance.
explanation:
**Oral intake support** includes food preferences, company at meals, feeding assistance, and minimizing dietary restrictions (p. 427). Hazzard describes "providing company at meals and feeding assistance as needed" (p. 427). Appetite-stimulant studies have not established improved functional outcomes in older adults, and mirtazapine lacks high-quality support for weight gain without depression (pp. 428-429).

**A. Use mirtazapine for weight gain without establishing depression.** Wrong, the source finds no high-quality evidence for weight gain from mirtazapine in the absence of depression (p. 429).
**B. Use megestrol for expected gains in function and quality of life.** Wrong, weight gain with these agents has not been associated with improved function or quality of life; megestrol also has significant adverse effects (p. 428).
**C. Use dronabinol for established clinical benefits in older adults.** Wrong, dronabinol has not been carefully studied in older adults and has shown at best limited promise in small nonrandomized trials (p. 428).
**D. Adjust the meal environment and provide feeding assistance.** Correct, environmental and feeding support are explicitly described approaches to improving oral intake (p. 427).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 427, 428, 429.
chapterTitle: Nutrition Disorders, Obesity, and Enteral/Parenteral Alimentation
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · pp.427–428

q: A 73-year-old woman with hypertension takes a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug for joint pain. What is the role of reviewing this medication in her blood pressure evaluation?
o: Identifying a medication contributing to elevated blood pressure
Identifying a medication providing an antihypertensive effect
Identifying a medication replacing repeated blood pressure measurements
Identifying a medication making standing blood pressure measurement unnecessary
explanation:
**Medication review** is part of evaluating potentially reversible contributors to hypertension. Hazzard includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs among implicated medications and separately requires appropriate repeated and positional blood pressure measurements (p. 1222). "A complete medication review is warranted to search for medications that may be implicated, for example, corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs including COX-2 inhibitors." (p. 1222).

**A. Identifying a medication contributing to elevated blood pressure.** Correct, the source names nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs among medications that may contribute to elevated pressure (p. 1222).
**B. Identifying a medication providing an antihypertensive effect.** Wrong, in this evaluation, the source identifies this drug class as a possible contributor to elevated pressure, rather than an antihypertensive treatment (p. 1222).
**C. Identifying a medication replacing repeated blood pressure measurements.** Wrong, the source requires repeated measurements for diagnosis; identifying a medication does not satisfy that measurement requirement (p. 1222).
**D. Identifying a medication making standing blood pressure measurement unnecessary.** Wrong, supine and upright readings assess a postural decrease in pressure, an assessment still required in the source (p. 1222).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1222.
ref: Hazzard Ch 79 — HYPERTENSION · Harrison Ch 243 — Approach to the Patient with Possible Cardiovascular Disease

q: An older woman receiving an opioid has constipation. Examination identifies a large, firm rectal impaction, without peritoneal signs or suspected perforation. According to Hazzard, what should precede insertion of an enema or suppository?
o: Administer a soapsuds enema to soften the impacted stool.
Begin docusate and wait for the impacted stool to pass.
Insert a suppository before attempting to remove the impaction.
Manually evacuate the large mass of hard rectal stool.
explanation:
**Manual evacuation** is the first step for a firm, large rectal impaction before enemas or suppositories. Docusate does not effectively treat constipation or rectal outlet delay in older people, and soapsuds enemas should not be administered to them (p. 1376).
"In patients who have a firm and large rectal impaction, manual evacuation should be performed before inserting enemas or suppositories," (p. 1376).

**A. Administer a soapsuds enema to soften the impacted stool.** Wrong, Hazzard advises against soapsuds enemas in older patients; the firm rectal mass also calls for manual evacuation first (p. 1376).
**B. Begin docusate and wait for the impacted stool to pass.** Wrong, docusate is ineffective for this constipation or outlet problem, and waiting omits the recommended initial evacuation (p. 1376).
**C. Insert a suppository before attempting to remove the impaction.** Wrong, the source places manual clearance before suppository insertion for a firm, large impaction (p. 1376).
**D. Manually evacuate the large mass of hard rectal stool.** Correct, this directly follows the source sequence for the rectal finding described (p. 1376).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1376.
ref: Hazzard Ch 87 — CONSTIPATION · Harrison Ch 49 — Diarrhea and Constipation

q: מה מאפיין את השינויים בלבלב בגיל המבוגר ?
o: יש ירידה בתפקוד האקסוקריני של הלבלב
יש עליה בנפח הלבלב משני להסננה שומנית
יש עליה בלחץ של ה- SPHINCTER OF ODI
יש ירידה במשקל הלבלב
explanation:
Aging is associated with **fat accumulation, fibrosis and reduced pancreatic weight**. Reduced exocrine secretion must be distinguished from clinically apparent insufficiency, which is not an inevitable consequence of healthy aging (Hazzard 8e, p. 1348).

**A. Pancreatic exocrine function decreases.** Wrong for official scoring, but the wording is broad. Hazzard describes declining bicarbonate and pancreatic fluid secretion, and the review reports functional decline in some studies. These findings must be distinguished from clinical exocrine insufficiency; they do not justify teaching that all function is always preserved (Hazzard, p. 1348; Löhr et al., Age-related changes in pancreatic function, Table 2).
**B. Pancreatic volume increases because of fatty infiltration.** Wrong, fat and fibrosis do not establish organ enlargement: Hazzard describes reduced weight, and the review describes decreasing parenchymal volume with age (Hazzard, p. 1348; Löhr et al., Abstract).
**C. Sphincter of Oddi pressure increases.** Wrong, the study summarized in the review found no age-related impairment in the secretin response and sphincter function assessed. This does not establish increased sphincter pressure as a general aging feature, nor should it be read as a direct pressure measurement in every population (Löhr et al., Age-related changes in pancreatic function, Table 2).
**D. Pancreatic weight decreases.** Correct, reduced weight is listed alongside fat and fibrosis in the aging table. This supports the official answer without implying that every structural change causes clinical insufficiency (Hazzard, p. 1348, Table 86-7).

Regarding reduced exocrine function: bicarbonate secretion declines with age, but clinical exocrine insufficiency is rare in healthy older adults. Pancreatic weight decreases after the seventh decade (Hazzard 8e, p. 1348).

Note: The option describing reduced exocrine function does not distinguish measurable secretion decline from clinical insufficiency. The key is preserved, and the explanation emphasizes this distinction rather than claiming that secretion does not decline.

Source: Hazzard 8e, p. 1348, Table 86-7; Löhr JM, Panic N, Vujasinovic M, Verbeke CS. The ageing pancreas: a systematic review of the evidence and analysis of the consequences. J Intern Med. 2018;283:446–460. doi:10.1111/joim.12745, Abstract, Age-related changes in pancreatic function and Table 2.

explanationSource.note: Checked v74 explanation sentences use Hazzard 8e; the printed IMA 7e reference is retained.

q: בן 87, סובל מסוכרת שנים רבות. מזה שנתיים ללא טיפול תרופתי. ברקע – מחלת אלצהיימר, גר עם מטפל צמוד ומתנייד עם הליכון. המטפל מדווח שהמטופל מרבה לשתות ומטיל שתן בתכיפות גדולה. ירד במשקל 6 ק"ג בחודשים האחרונים. במעבדה המוגלובין A1C – 11%. על פי המאמר ADA Older Adults: Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes-2022 מה הטיפול המומלץ?
o: התחלת טיפול באינסולין ארוך טווח וטיטרציה עד לשיפור בתסמיני ההיפרגליקמיה
מעקב ערכי סוכר 3 פעמים ביום והתאמת טיפול באינסולין קצר טווח לפי טבלה
בגילו ובמצבו אין צורך להקפיד על איזון סוכרת
התחלת טיפול באנלוגים של GLP1 ומעכבי SGLT2
explanation:
In a patient with dementia and symptomatic hyperglycemia, the goal is **symptom relief while avoiding hypoglycemia**. Table 13.2 supports simplifying treatment, and the article presents **once-daily basal insulin** as a reasonable option in older patients, titrated to the individual goal (ADA Older Adults, 2022, Table 13.2 and Insulin Therapy).

**A. Start long-acting insulin and titrate until hyperglycemic symptoms improve.** Correct, this applies a simple regimen that can address symptoms with caregiver support, careful titration, and avoidance of hypoglycemia (Table 13.2; Insulin Therapy).
**B. Check glucose three times daily and adjust short-acting insulin using a sliding scale.** Wrong, repeated calculations and injections add complexity; the source recommends matching complexity to functional and cognitive ability and simplifying when needed (Table 13.2; Insulin Therapy).
**C. At his age and in his condition, diabetes control is unnecessary.** Wrong, avoiding tight control does not mean leaving symptomatic hyperglycemia untreated; the source explicitly identifies symptomatic hyperglycemia as something to avoid (Table 13.2).
**D. Start GLP-1 analogues and SGLT2 inhibitors.** Wrong, as the best choice here. The article cautions that GLP-1 receptor agonists may not be preferred with unexplained weight loss and notes volume depletion and worsening urinary incontinence with SGLT2 inhibitors in older patients, relevant to this patient's symptoms (Incretin-Based Therapies; SGLT2 Inhibitors).

Source: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. Older Adults: Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes—2022. Diabetes Care. 2022;45(Suppl 1):S195-S207, Table 13.2; Insulin Therapy; Incretin-Based Therapies; SGLT2 Inhibitors, doi:10.2337/dc22-S013.
